nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-born British; Anglo-Irish, and the Whig parliamentary oratory and the political and aesthetic prose of the later eighteenth century
literary_identity: Statesman, political writer and philosophical critic of the passions; the Rockingham Whig parliamentarian and manager of the Hastings impeachment, whose Reflections on the Revolution in France became the classic English argument against the French Revolution, and whose Enquiry of 1757 supplied the period's standard analysis of the sublime and the beautiful.
biography: Burke was born in Dublin in 1729, the son of a solicitor who conformed to the church of Ireland and of Mary Nagle of a Cork Catholic family; brought up in his father's communion but kept on friendly terms with his Catholic kindred, he entered Trinity College Dublin, and removed to London and the Middle Temple about 1750, where he abandoned the law for letters. His first books made his name: A Vindication of Natural Society (1756), a sceptical exposure of civil government which many readers mistook for a grave attack on revelation, and the Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful (1757). Through the publisher Robert Dodsley he founded the Annual Register and wrote its historical and critical survey of Europe for many years. He entered the Commons in 1761 as member for Wendover, was private secretary to Rockingham in the administration of 1765-66, and in the Thoughts on the Cause of the Present Discontents (1770) turned party connexion into a doctrine of organised principled opposition. Member for Bristol from 1774, he argued in his address of that year and in the Speech on Conciliation with America of 1775 that a representative owes his unbiased judgement to his constituents, not his obedience. He bought the estate of Gregories near Beaconsfield in 1768 and lived thereafter in permanent tension between country propriety and heavy borrowing. Paymaster of the Forces in the Rockingham ministry of 1782, he became the manager of the impeachment of Warren Hastings, which he opened in Westminster Hall in 1788 and which filled the rest of his public life. The French Revolution broke his long alliance with Charles James Fox; the Reflections on the Revolution in France of November 1790, the Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs of 1791 and the Letters on a Regicide Peace of 1795-97 made him the most read and most attacked political writer of the war years. He retired from the Commons in 1794 and died at Beaconsfield in 1797, buried at Gerrards Cross. The death of his only son Richard in 1794 darkened his last years, and unfinished pieces on the revolution and on Shakespeare were published after his death.
literary_profile: His writings form three connected bodies: the early philosophical treatise, the parliamentary speech and printed letter, and the great state paper of the impeachment. The Philosophical Enquiry states a theory of the sublime and the beautiful as passions rooted in self-preservation and in society, and its divisions on the passions, on the sublime, on the beautiful and on the effect of general and obscure notions became the received framework of aesthetic discussion in the 1790s. The Annual Register's annual historical and critical articles made it the standard English chronicle of European affairs for two generations. The Reflections is a letter of remonstrance and prophecy that mixes constitutional argument with the elevated lament; the speeches on America and on the conduct of the East India manager are oratory revised into printed state papers; the Letters on a Regicide Peace argue publicly and at great length against a settlement with revolutionary France.
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of sustained periodic sentence in which abstraction is embodied in image and in moral feeling, and argument advances by concession, by historical instance and by the accumulating weight of clause upon clause. He can be plainly businesslike in a minute or a resolution, ironical in definition, and torrential in the rhetorical burst, of which the passage on the queen of France in the Reflections is the most quoted and most imitated specimen in English. The characteristic movement is nevertheless the long qualification and the appeal to prescriptive usage, the concrete enumeration of institutions and orders. In the treatise the manner is analytic and deliberately dry; in the speeches judicial and cumulative; in the late pamphlets urgent, and occasionally uneven with anger.
intellectual_concerns: Liberty as an inherited and prescriptive estate rather than an abstract speculable right; the moral limits of empire and the duties and accountability of power; party, connexion and principled opposition as the conditions of constitutional freedom; the dangers of an armed metaphysics and of geometric abstraction in politics; the civilising uses of prejudice, of religious establishment and of the learned and gentle orders; the passions of the sublime and of beauty, and the effect of obscurity and sympathy; the prudence and historical consequence that should govern imperial and foreign policy.
historical_significance: The Reflections created the durable language of modern political conservatism and supplied the founding text of the anti-Jacobin answer to 1789, at which Paine's Rights of Man and Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Men were aimed; the Enquiry fixed the terms of the debate on the sublime for two generations of artists and writers. His speeches and letters are the central English documents on the American and Indian questions, and his management of the impeachment established the doctrine of public accountability in colonial government. His account of party and of the independence of the representative remains the standard statement of eighteenth-century Whig parliamentary practice.
biographical_uncertainty: His Dublin birthplace is not in question, though the street of his birth is variously identified and the day is usually given as 12 January 1729. The day of his death is reported now as the ninth and now as the end of July 1797 in different calendars, and his house is described sometimes at Beaconsfield and sometimes at Gregories in that parish. His matriculation and degree at Trinity College Dublin, the chronology of his removal to London and of his keeping in the Temple are set down with small variations in the biographies. The extent of his share in the earliest volumes of the Annual Register, and the responsibility for the anonymously printed pieces of the 1750s, remain matters of bibliographical inference rather than of documented fact.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the provincial medical and scientific writing of the Gloucestershire country practitioners, and the empirical pamphlet literature of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries
literary_identity: Country physician and naturalist, and the founder of vaccination; a writer of short, plain, evidence-driven medical pamphlets whose Inquiry of 1798 is one of the most consequential scientific books in English, and whose published work sits beside a large unpublished record of observation on birds, geology and the natural history of the Severn vale.
biography: Jenner was born at Berkeley in Gloucestershire on 17 May 1749, the son of the vicar of Berkeley, the Rev. Stephen Jenner, and lost his parents while still a child. He was put out at about thirteen to a neighbouring surgeon-apothecary at Sodbury, and served his apprenticeship in that practice before removing to London, where he lodged and studied, attended the lectures and the house practice at St George's Hospital, and worked under John Hunter, whose experimental method he adopted. Admitted a member of the Royal College of Surgeons in 1773, he returned to Berkeley and settled there in practice, in a country partnership which gave him the range of cases, and the leisured observation, on which his later work was built; he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1788. His inquiry into the cowpox of the Gloucestershire dairies grew out of the common belief of the dairy women, that infection with the cow's distemper protected against smallpox. On 14 May 1796 he inoculated with cowpox matter taken from the hand of Sarah Nelmes, a dairymaid, James Phipps, the young son of his gardener, and afterwards tested the boy's immunity by variolous matter. The results were published in London in 1798 in a small self-printed volume, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, a Disease Discovered in Some of the Western Counties of England, Particularly Gloucestershire, and Known by the Name of the Cow Pox, which established the practice of vaccination and gave it its name. The book was attacked, ridiculed and answered in pamphlets, and was also adopted rapidly on the Continent and in the Americas; Jenner continued to publish the progress of the new practice, supplied vaccine matter gratuitously to inquirers and correspondents, and prosecuted his observations on the migration and habits of the swallow and on other natural-history questions. His wife Catherine died in 1815; his own health failed after a mild stroke in 1822, and he died at Berkeley on 26 January 1823, buried in the church there. The practice he founded became the basis of immunology and of the public vaccination programmes of the century.
literary_profile: His published medical writing is short, practical and cumulative rather than systematic: the Inquiry of 1798, a plain statement of cases arranged as evidence, with the history of the cow-pox, the account of the experiments on Phipps and on other persons, and the anatomical and clinical description of the vesicle; the Continuation of Facts and Observations relative to the Variolae Vaccinae of 1800; and The Origin of the Vaccine Inoculation of 1801, a summary of the case against variolation. To these belong his introductory letters to correspondents, his papers to the Royal Society, and his observations on the natural history of the rook and the swallow, published separately and in the philosophical transactions of the day. He wrote also an account of his own inoculations and a pamphlet of popular instruction, and left the manuscripts and notebooks of a lifelong naturalist.
stylistic_characteristics: A spare, unornamented and avowedly diffident prose of case, date and outcome, in which the claim is carried by the enumeration of instances and by the repetition of the same experiment on different persons, with a deliberate refusal of theory. He writes plainly and even homely, names his informants and their parishes, dates each case, and reserves his judgement to the shortest possible conclusion; the polemic against his opponents, when it appears, is cool, factual and occasionally wry. His natural-history writing shares the same habits of close observation of particular creatures in a particular country.
intellectual_concerns: The relation of cattle disease to human infection, and the specific protection given by one disease against another; the trial of an hypothesis by a single designed experiment and its repetition; the immunity produced by cow-pox and its duration; the comparison of vaccination with the dangerous practice of inserting smallpox matter; the safety and public diffusion of a cheap remedy; the honest reporting of failed and anomalous cases; the natural history, habits and migration of the birds and animals of the Gloucestershire vale.
historical_significance: The Inquiry of 1798 founded vaccination and gave preventive medicine its first rational procedure; within a few years the practice spread through Europe and the Americas, was adopted by governments and public institutions, and displaced the older variolation, preparing the way for the eradication of smallpox announced in the twentieth century. His method, an hypothesis tested by inoculation and by subsequent challenge with the dangerous matter, became a model of experimental medicine, and the derivation of that method from John Hunter's practice is the best-known instance in English of the country physician changing the practice of a whole society. He is also a figure of literary history, since the controversy over vaccination filled the pamphlet and cartoon literature of the Regency years.
major_influences: the Gloucestershire dairy farmers and country observers whose reports he collected
biographical_uncertainty: The details of his apprenticeship and of the Sodbury years, and the chronology of his London study with Hunter at St George's, are given with small variations in the memoirs, which depend heavily on his own notebooks and on the family Life written by his early biographer John Baron. The order of the first cowpox experiments is sometimes told so as to make the 1796 Phipps case the sole decisive instance, whereas his earlier local observations and the trial on his own children are variously dated; and the exact priority of the dairymaid Sarah Nelmes's infection, and of the accounts of farmers and physicians who had practised something like vaccination before him, remains disputed. The day of his death is given as 26 January 1823.

birthplace: London (Red Lion Street, Holborn); removed in infancy to Lavenham, Suffolk
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the dissenting and evangelical nursery verse of the early nineteenth century, and the moral essay and tale written for children and domestic periodicals
literary_identity: Nursery poet, hymn-writer and moral essayist; the younger of the Miss Taylors, whose joint Original Poems for Infant Minds rebuilt the English verse addressed to very young children, and the author of the poem 'The Star', known ever afterwards as 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star'.
biography: Jane Taylor was born in London on 23 September 1783, the second of the eleven children of Isaac Taylor, a portrait-engraver of some reputation who turned to the dissenting ministry, and whose family removed to Lavenham in Suffolk while she was an infant, her father being settled there over a congregation. She was educated at home in a household of engravers, ministers and writers, and her printed work began in close collaboration with her elder sister Ann, who was her companion in authorship all her life. In 1804 the London firm of Darton published Original Poems for Infant Minds by the two Miss Taylors; the book was taken up at once by the evangelical and dissenting nursery and went through many editions. Rhymes for the Nursery followed in 1806, and in it appeared 'The Star', the poem which, set afterwards to an air from a French collection of melodies, became the most widely reprinted and best-known nursery rhyme in English. Hymns for Infant Minds of 1810 continued the same joint work. The earlier volumes were issued anonymously or under initials, and were read for a long time as the utterance of a single nursery voice. From about 1810, when the family removed from Lavenham, Jane's life was that of a dependent unmarried woman among her relatives, with long stays at Colchester, at Marazion in Cornwall, and at Ongar in Essex, where a brother held a ministry; her health steadily failed under constant literary work. She wrote increasingly in prose as well as in verse: Display of 1814, a set of tales and illustrations on the power of truth which reached several editions; Essays in Rhyme, on Morals and Manners of 1816; and the papers contributed to the Youth's Magazine which were collected after her writing as Contributions of Q. Q. to a Periodical Work. She died at Ongar in Essex on 13 April 1824 and was buried there, and her Memoir and Letters were published by friends and kindred, while her sister Ann outlived her by more than forty years and became herself a familiar religious writer.
literary_profile: Her work is an infant and nursery literature made deliberately: short poems in the simplest metres, addressed to children of two to seven, on small animals, on servants and children, on the weather, sleep and the duties of the family, together with hymns, and with prose tales and essays in which children reason their way out of a false step. The joint volumes of Original Poems for Infant Minds and Rhymes for the Nursery are the core, the former more narrative and argumentative, the latter more purely rhyming; Hymns for Infant Minds adapts the same diction to devotional use. Display, the Essays in Rhyme and the magazine papers signed Q. Q. extend the method into the essay and the tale, with a constant didactic aim and an unusual attention to the mind of the reader addressed.
stylistic_characteristics: An extremely plain, light and conversational verse of short lines, of nursery rhyming couplet and ballad stanza, with a fondness for the question addressed to the child, for the personified small creature, and for the easy moral turn in the closing couplet. Her compression, the perfect fit of sound to sense, and the absence of archaism and of ornament give the best of her poems their lasting hold on memory. Her prose is clear, domestic, quietly humorous and didactic without declamation, nearer to the familiar essay and the tale than to the sermon; in the hymns and the graver verse a cooler and more reflective manner appears.
intellectual_concerns: The infant mind as a thing to be studied and not merely governed; the moral training of pity, truthfulness and self-command through the smallest daily incidents; the place of religion, of the natural world and of the family in a child's first knowledge; the claims and dignity of servants and dependents; the danger of false feeling in children's books, and the duty of writing to the actual capacities of the reader addressed.
historical_significance: With her sister she created the standard English nursery book of the nineteenth century: the Original Poems and the Rhymes were the volumes from which generations of children learned to read, and 'The Star' passed into a global children's song and is the single most quoted poem of the period's writing for the young. Her method of addressing the child's own mind helped to move English children's literature from instruction toward observation, and her prose and magazine work belongs to the large dissenting literature of domestic education which links the Edgeworth circle to the Victorian nursery.
major_influences: Isaac Taylor, her father, and the dissenting and evangelical nursery tradition
the English hymn and moral-tale writers of the religious book-societies
Maria Edgeworth and the familiar educational prose of the 1790s
biographical_uncertainty: Her birthplace is given in most popular accounts as Lavenham in Suffolk, and in the modern scholarly and family record as Red Lion Street, Holborn, London, the family having removed to Lavenham in her infancy; the day is recorded as 23 September 1783. The division of authorship between the two sisters in the joint volumes of 1804 to 1810, which were published anonymously or under initials, is still not settled piece by piece, and the constant attribution of 'The Star' to Jane rests on family tradition and publisher's records rather than on a signed first text. The order and dates of her later residences, and the year in which her share in the nursery volumes came to be distinguished from her sister's, vary in the memoirs written by relatives.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Irish; the provincial improvement and educational writing of the later eighteenth century, and the natural-philosophical and inventive culture of the Midlands and of Ireland
literary_identity: Landowner, inventor, engineer and educational theorist; the Irish country gentleman of the Lunar Society circle who made the government of a great family and the training of infant minds an experiment, and whose Practical Education and household tales, written with his daughter Maria, form one of the most original pedagogic enterprises of the 1790s.
biography: Edgeworth was born at Bath in 1744, the son of an Anglo-Irish family with estates in Longford, and was educated afterwards at Trinity College Dublin and for a short time at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He came into the family estate at Edgeworthstown in Longford and spent the rest of his life as an Irish country landlord, engineer and improver. He married four times, the wives being Anna Maria Elers, Honora Sneyd, Honora's sister Elizabeth Sneyd, and, in 1798, Frances Ann Beaufort; by them he left a very large family, many of whom died young, and among his surviving children the eldest was Maria, afterwards the novelist. He belonged to the Birmingham circle afterwards known as the Lunar Society, and worked and corresponded with James Watt, Joseph Priestley, Erasmus Darwin and Matthew Boulton. His inventions, which he recorded at length, were serious rather than fortunate: a copying and measuring machine, a steam-carriage and road-making scheme he described as a cart carrying its own road, a telegraph, a method of teaching the deaf, and improvements in the roads and drains of Ireland. He was employed on canal and harbour surveys, and published a treatise on road-making and a plan for teaching arithmetic by self-instruction. In politics he was a reforming Irish Protestant who urged concession to the Catholics and a limited parliamentary reform, and who opposed the Act of Union of 1800. After the death of his second wife he undertook the education of his children as an experiment in the training of the understanding, conducted at Edgeworthstown with Maria as his closest collaborator. The method was printed in Practical Education of 1798, stated on its title page as the work of Miss Edgeworth and her father, and followed by the Essays on Professional Education of 1809 and by Readings on Poetry of 1816; the household stories out of which it grew were published as The Parent's Assistant in 1796 in his daughter's name, and the plan of instruction for the youngest children appeared afterwards as Early Lessons. He wrote his own Memoirs, which Maria completed and published in 1820, and he died at Edgeworthstown on 13 June 1817.
literary_profile: His books are practical and experimental: the educational treatises, the scientific and engineering papers, the political pamphlets on Irish affairs, and the household narratives. Practical Education, in two volumes, argues from the history of his own children's teaching that the powers of the mind are formed by association and use, and its chapters on reading, writing, grammar, natural philosophy and the classics are illustrated with the small facts of a family experiment; the Essays on Professional Education carry the same method into the training of the professions, and Readings on Poetry applies it to literary teaching. The Memoirs are an autobiography of inventions, friendships and family, written without reserve and finished by his daughter. To these belong his account of road-making, his papers on the copying and telegraph machines, and the plans for the instruction of the deaf and for teaching arithmetic.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, quick, argumentative prose of the laboratory and the estate, full of named instances, of the small concrete cases from which a principle is drawn, and of a self-conscious candour about his own failures; the educational writing is conversational and domestic, addressed to parents, and it turns the anecdote into evidence. The Memoirs add a garrulous and impatient first-person manner, in which invention, friendship and family grief are told in one breath; the scientific and political pamphlets are drier, more technical, and given to numbered proposals and to the estimate of cost.
intellectual_concerns: The formation of the infant understanding by association, use and self-instruction rather than by memory and fear; the education of judgement for the professions and for public life; the invention and practical application of machines, and the useful arts of road, canal and harbour making; the improvement and government of an Irish estate and of a largely Catholic tenantry; the claims of religious toleration and parliamentary reform in Ireland; the uses of emulation, of conversation and of the child's own curiosity in teaching; the relation of scientific friendship to literary work.
historical_significance: He gave the English education of the nineteenth century one of its founding ideas, that the mind is to be studied in the actual child and trained by the management of association, and Practical Education, whatever the share of his daughter in its authorship, made that idea widely known and was read and answered through the century. His household tales founded the realistic domestic story for children, and the long Memoirs are an indispensable record of the Lunar Society, of Watt and the midlands philosophers, and of Irish improvement and politics between the American and the French wars.
biographical_uncertainty: The number of his children is variously given in the accounts, and the names and dates of his four marriages are recorded with small differences, the usual order being Anna Maria Elers, Honora Sneyd, Elizabeth Sneyd and Frances Ann Beaufort. The dating and the division of work between father and daughter in The Parent's Assistant and in Practical Education remain the subject of scholarship rather than of settled record, since the books appeared under his daughter's name or under a joint designation; and the value of his own account of his inventions, and of his share in the inventions attributed to Watt and to others, cannot be measured independently of the Memoirs, which are necessarily self-reporting. The chronology of his college years at Durham, Dublin and Oxford is imperfectly documented.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Welsh-born British; the Owenite and cooperative writing of the early industrial decades, and the Welsh-English prose of social reform, report and autobiography
literary_identity: Cotton manufacturer, manager of New Lanark and social reformer; the writer who turned the government of a manufacturing community into a published argument for character, education and cooperation, and whose pamphlets, reports and autobiography founded the Owenite movement of the 1830s and 1840s.
biography: Owen was born at Newtown in Montgomeryshire on 14 May 1771, the son of a saddler and ironmonger, and was apprenticed as a draper in London in early youth. He bought his way out of service, took a share in a Manchester manufacturing business, and taught himself the theory and practice of cotton spinning. In 1799 or 1800 he became a partner in, and manager of, the cotton works at New Lanark on the Clyde, founded by David Dale whose daughter he had married, and there for a quarter of a century he carried out the experiment that made his name: a shortened working day, the refusal to take children under ten into the mills, an infant school and schools for the older children, company shops, housing, saving banks and insurance, and the deliberate government of the population as a moral and educational concern. New Lanark was visited by foreign observers and by statistical inquirers, and Owen published his practice in A New View of Society of 1813, which was widely translated. His success in manufacture he now turned against the system of competition. At the request of the magistrates and clergy of his adopted county he drew up the Report to the County of Lanark, printed at Glasgow in 1821, which argued from the distress and surplus labour of the post-war years for villages of cooperation and mutual interest to be raised by parishes, counties and the state, and which offered his famous national plan of education and production to Parliament. Disappointed in Britain, he bought the settlement of New Harmony in Indiana and removed thither in 1825 with his sons and a company of friends; the experiment failed in a few years and left him heavy losses and an unpopularity he never wholly overcame. He returned to Britain, settled in London, and spent the rest of his life as a public teacher of cooperation, lecturing, printing and organising, and giving his countenance to cooperative communities and to the trade unions of 1834. His Book of the New Moral World gathered his later teaching; his Autobiography, revised by his son, was published in the 1850s. He died at Newtown, where he had been born, on 17 November 1858, and was buried there.
literary_profile: His writings are those of a reformer and a manager rather than a literary artist: the New View of Society of 1813, a series of short argumentative essays on the formation of character, on the vice of the existing system and on the means of its remedial change; the Report to the County of Lanark of 1821, a statistical and practical proposal of villages of cooperation, written for a county meeting and printed with the returns of population and distress; a great body of addresses, letters, open letters to ministers and to governments, and evidence before committees; the Book of the New Moral World, in which his later teaching on society, production and religion was systematically set out; and the Autobiography, the plainest and most readable of his books, which records his boyhood, his apprenticeship and his management of New Lanark.
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, urgent, unprefaced prose of proposition and proof, written in short numbered paragraphs and in the vocabulary of fact, of experience and of common sense; he reasons from the case of his own mills, uses figures and returns of population, wages and product, and is confident to the point of dogma, with a marked habit of addressing parliaments, counties and nations directly. The Autobiography is conversational, unaffected and anecdotal, with a dissenting plainness of statement; his later polemical writing grows repetitive, abstract and missionary.
intellectual_concerns: The formation of character by circumstance, education and example, and therefore the irresponsibility of punishing the vices produced by bad institutions; the moral government and education of a manufacturing population, and the infant school as the key to social change; the waste, cruelty and instability of competition and of the cheap-labour system; the village or community of cooperation and mutual interest as the unit of reorganised production; the surplus labour and distress of the peace; the public duty of the state, the parish and the rich in education and in the relief of the poor; the relation of religion, of marriage and of property to social improvement.
historical_significance: He made New Lanark the best-known example in Europe of the manufacturer's management of his people, and his Formation of Character and his Report to the County of Lanark set the terms on which education, the relief of distress and model communities were argued in the 1820s; his name gave the cooperative movement its most powerful English organising impulse, and the villages of cooperation he proposed were the parent of the Owenite communities of the 1820s and 1830s in Britain and America. His teaching, his lectures and his sponsorship of the trade union and cooperative enterprises of 1834 stand between the philanthropic paternalism of the eighteenth century and the organised labour and cooperative movement of the nineteenth, and the Autobiography remains a founding text of the working-man's own record of industrial life.
major_influences: the practical philanthropy of David Dale and of Arkwright's mills
Jeremy Bentham and the utilitarian argument on circumstances
the Quaker and Welsh dissenting environment of his childhood
biographical_uncertainty: The year in which he became a partner at New Lanark is given as 1799 and as 1800, the difference turning on the date of the written agreement and of his taking up the management. His first publication, the New View of Society, is generally dated from the private printing of 1812 and the public edition of 1813, and the Report to the County of Lanark is described both as composed for the county meeting of 1820 and as printed in 1821. The numbers he gives of the New Lanark population, of his returns and of the losses at New Harmony are his own report and cannot be independently verified, and the extent to which his later writings were drafted or revised by his sons and by his secretary is not settled.
